prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology, tasks and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: B013 is the candidate that best meets the standard of new evidence plus an explanatory framework. The Katz-Murphy supply-and-demand view of the wage structure and the task-based approach give a conceptual account of why returns to skill and routine work moved as they did. The China-shock design adds credible, transparent identification of local labour-market adjustment, and the whole programme created new measurement and a research agenda that others have taken up. It concerns a first-order question about who gains and loses from technology and trade, and it has influenced both research and public debate. The core empirical patterns have been replicated and extended over roughly three decades, so the timing is ripe. Having reread the other openings, I still rank it first on merit. I rank B001 and B002 close behind and would not regard either as a poor outcome.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is the main weakness. The work has two strands, the technology and task framework and the trade-shock evidence, and the three-name cap forces a choice. Dorn is as central to the China-shock papers as Hanson or Katz is to their strands. The task framework also shares intellectual ground with Acemoglu's 2024 recognition and with authors outside the credited list. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated. By comparison, B001 has a more compact attribution (BLP plus Pakes's dynamic-industry work) and a longer record of adoption in regulatory practice.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B013 second and names Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She says the China-shock evidence is mainly Autor-Dorn-Hanson and that Katz's credit is spread across the task and skill-premium strands. She also sees overlap with the 2023 prize and the Katz/Goldin lineage.
responses.response: I agree that Dorn's claim on the China-shock strand matches Hanson's, and that Katz's credit is spread. I keep Katz because the skill-premium and education-technology framework is the explanatory half of the programme, and without him the prize becomes mostly a trade-shock prize. I do not think the 2023 prize overlaps in a way that matters. It rewarded the historical evidence on women's labour-market outcomes, not wage-structure or displacement. I accept that Autor-Hanson-Dorn is a defensible alternative trio. The choice between Katz and Dorn is a real attribution decision for the Committee, and I have no way of making it free of judgment.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B013 fifth with Autor and Katz only. He questions whether it is empirical documentation rather than conceptual discovery, and he notes overlap with Acemoglu's 2024 prize area. He ranks B001 first on durability and wide use of the tools.
responses.response: I take the documentation concern seriously. I think the task framework, together with the Katz-Murphy relative-supply logic, supplies the conceptual component, and the trade-shock papers test a specific mechanism and do not merely describe patterns. Where I partly agree is on attribution. A two-name Autor-Katz award is cleaner on credit but drops the trade-shock design, which is the part that changed policy debate. I also grant that B001 has the stronger record on durability and wide adoption. My remaining reservation about it is that it is mostly a toolkit prize, and committees weigh toolkits and discoveries differently. That is a difference in judgment and not a merit gap I can establish.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B001 first as a structural-estimation tradition not yet recognised. He proposes Autor and Hanson alone for B013, and notes that the task framework also runs through Acemoglu, who has already been recognised.
responses.response: The Acemoglu point is fair, and it is a reason to define the B013 citation by the wage-structure and trade-exposure evidence and not as a general prize for the task framework. I disagree with the two-name version. Leaving out Katz's long-run work on the relative demand for skill would remove the part of the programme with the longest confirmation. I agree with Hassler's maturity argument for B001, and it persuades me that B001 is the strongest alternative. I would not support B001 over B013 only because it has more first-place rankings, since counts do not measure scientific merit.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B002 first. He calls the collateral-amplification mechanism deep and general, and he flags the 2022 overlap and the Gertler/Gilchrist question.
responses.response: I ranked B002 second for similar reasons. Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean originating contribution and was reinforced by 2008. My hesitation is the same as his: Bernanke's 2022 prize covers neighbouring ground, and the Gertler/Gilchrist boundary is hard to draw. It also depends more on theory than B013 does, because the empirical identification of the collateral channel is less direct. I think B013 has the cleaner link between evidence and framework, but the gap with B002 is small and a reasonable member could reverse it.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the technology/task strand and the trade-shock strand as one achievement, and so how the three names split among Autor, Katz, Hanson and Dorn.
How far the China-shock magnitudes and long-run interpretation have settled, and how much the Acemoglu 2024 recognition limits the novelty of the task framework.
Whether the Committee would prefer B001, with its compact credit and long adoption record, to B013 on attribution and maturity grounds. I have not independently verified citation or adoption data.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot entry. I use administrative data in my own work, which is methodologically close to B017, but I have no connection to its candidates and B017 is not in my preferred configuration.
